title: BVA Decision 25000007: Entitlement to service connection for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is granted
text:
Citation Nr: 25000007
Decision Date: 01/02/25	Archive Date: 01/02/25

DOCKET NO. 19-22 400
DATE: January 2, 2025

ORDER

Entitlement to service connection for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is granted. 

Entitlement to service connection for gastroenteritis is denied.  

FINDINGS OF FACT

1. The Veteran's GERD is due to service.

2. Gastroenteritis is not shown to be causally or etiologically related to any disease, injury, or incident during service.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The criteria for entitlement to service connection for GERD have been met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1101, 1110, 1112, 1113, 1116, 1137, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.303, 3.304, 3.310. 

2. The criteria for service connection for gastroenteritis have not been met.  38 U.S.C. §§ 1101, 1110, 1137, 5107; 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.102, 3.303, 3.307, 3.309.

REASONS AND BASES FOR FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The appellant is a Veteran who served on active duty from November 1967 to December 1970 and from April 1973 to October 1992.  This matter is before the Board of Veterans' Appeals (Board) on appeal from a rating decision from the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Regional Office (RO). 

In March 2022, a Video Conference Board hearing was held before the undersigned.  A transcript of the hearing is associated with the Veteran's claims file.

In October 2023, the Board remanded these claims for additional development.  The requested action has been taken and the case was returned to the Board for adjudication.

Service Connection

Military personnel records confirm service in the Republic of Vietnam and Southwest (SW) Asia during the Persian Gulf War.

Service in Vietnam has been conceded.  In the case of veterans who have been exposed to an herbicide agent during active service, 38 C.F.R. § 3.309(e) generally provides for presumptive service connection for certain listed diseases, which listed diseases do not include dermatitis, gastroenteritis, or GERD.  See also 38 U.S.C. § 1116.  

A veteran may nevertheless prove entitlement to service connection on a direct basis due to herbicide exposure.  See Combee v. Brown, 5 Vet. App. 248 (1993); Stefl v. Nicholson, 21 Vet. App. 120 (2007) (holding that the availability of presumptive service connection for some conditions based on exposure to Agent Orange does not preclude direct service connection for other conditions based on exposure to Agent Orange).  

The Veteran served in the Southwest Asia theater of operations in support of Persian Gulf War.  38 C.F.R. § 3.317(e).  Under those provisions, service connection may be established for objective indications of a chronic disability resulting from an undiagnosed illness or illnesses, provided that such disability (1) became manifest in service on active duty in the Armed Forces in the Southwest Asia theater of operations during the Persian Gulf War; and (2) by history, physical examination, and laboratory tests cannot be attributed to a known clinical diagnosis.  38 U.S.C. § 1117; 38 C.F.R. § 3.317.

At the Board hearing, he reported his service in Vietnam and Saudi Arabia, and related his conditions may be related to either tour.  VA has conceded that the Veteran participated in a Toxic Exposure Risk Activity (TERA) during his military service. 

1. Entitlement to service connection for GERD

In February 1974, the Veteran was noted to have gastroenteritis, with the etiology undetermined.  In April 1975, he had complaints of stomach pain for 3 to 4 days and was noted to have a history of peptic ulcer disease.  In September 1979, he complained of severe stomach pain and discomfort.  He had classic peptic ulcer disease symptoms of epigastric pain.  He reported chronic mid-epigastric pain since 1967.  In November 1979, he was noted to have a peptic ulcer with severe pyloric spasm.  He was noted to have a long history of dyspepsia dating back many years.    

In January 2018, he underwent an esophageal examination.  He reported being diagnosed with GERD during service, however, review of the STRs did not support this contention.  He was diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease during service and had been taking Tagamet for the condition which is also the same medication to treat GERD.  He had an EGD in November 1979 which showed duodenal ulcer, but with no mention of GERD.  The examiner stated there are no objective findings of chronic GERD, and concluded it is less likely as not that the Veteran's current GI complaints were caused by or related to service.  

VAMC records note in September 2018 and March 2019 a diagnosis of GERD, and treatment of famotidine, which he was taking nightly to treat stomach acid.

At the Board hearing he reported experiencing gastrointestinal discomfort during service that has continued to present.  He is in receipt of service connection for a duodenal ulcer.

In January 2023, the Veteran underwent an examination.  The examiner detailed the Veteran's inservice treatment for peptic ulcer disease and a duodenal ulcer, however, the examiner found no indication of GERD during service.  The Veteran had no complaints of heartburn, acid regurgitation, or reflux during service.  The examiner indicated the Veteran had no signs or symptoms due to an esophageal condition, to include GERD; concluding GERD is less likely than not proximately due to or the result of service.  The Veteran is prescribed famotidine which is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and GERD; however, the records do not show for which pathology famotidine was prescribed.  A UGI in September 1979 was normal, and an EGD in November 1979 showed duodenal ulcer or with no mention of GERD or esophagitis.  Therefore, GERD was less likely than not caused by his duodenal ulcer.  The claimed GERD was less likely than not aggravated beyond natural progression by the duodenal ulcer.  The rationale is there is no pathology consistent with GERD found.  

In a July 2023 addendum, the examiner concluded gastroenteritis and GERD are less likely than not related to service.  The examiner explained there is no current chronic condition of gastroenteritis or GERD found on exam, and the conditions are not known to be caused by herbicide exposure.   

The examiner found that GERD was less likely than not due to an undiagnosed illness or medically unexplained chronic multi-symptom illness resulting from service in SW Asia.  The examiner found that the Veteran does not have GERD and/or gastroenteritis but noted that he is currently taking medications to treat gastrointestinal symptoms.  The examiner did not however, clarify the nature of these gastrointestinal symptoms and whether they could be the result of service in SW Asia.

In a November 2023 opinion, the examiner stated the Veteran does not have an intestinal condition.  He is currently prescribed famotidine, which is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, esophagitis, and GERD.  The records do not show for which pathology famotidine is prescribed.  As to GERD, the examiner stated GERD is a disease with a clear and specific etiology and diagnosis and happens when your lower esophageal sphincter becomes weak or relaxes when it should not, causing stomach contents to rise up into the esophagus.  Therefore, GERD is less likely due to an undiagnosed illness or medically unexplained chronic multi-symptom illness resulting from service in Southwest Asia during the Persian Gulf War.  Further the examiner concluded the Veteran does have a history of GERD as indicated by the January 2023 disability benefits questionnaire.  

In May 2024, the Veteran underwent an examination and was diagnosed with GERD and a duodenal ulcer.  

In a separate May 2024 opinion, the examiner noted the Veteran's medical history and his reports of heartburn, acidic taste in mouth, and nausea, and treatment with Famotidine.  The examiner explained the Veteran has GERD, which is a disease with a clear and specific etiology and diagnosis.  Further, GERD was less likely than not caused by the indicated toxic exposure risk activity.  Additionally, the examiner explained, though there is evidence of an association between GERD and TERA exposure in the medical literature, there is no objective finding to support direct causation.  Outside risk factors, stress and being overweight, would outweigh risks identified by TERA, in which there are none.   

In a September 2024 addendum, the examiner indicated the Veteran did not have GERD. 

In a November 2024 addendum, the examiner indicated the Veteran did have GERD.  The examiner concluded the Veteran's GERD diagnosis is considered chronic gastrointestinal disability of known etiology; therefore, it is not presumed to be due to his Persian Gulf service. 

The Veteran reported symptoms of dyspepsia and epigastric pain during service.  2018 and 20199 VA treatment records confirm a diagnosis of GERD.  He has consistently reported gastrointestinal discomfort since service.  A Veteran is also competent to testify regarding facts or circumstances that can be observed and described by a layperson.  

The May 2024 examining provider noted the Veteran's medical history, the Veteran's diagnosis of GERD, and treatment with Famotidine.  The examiner concluded GERD was less likely than not caused by the indicated toxic exposure risk activity.  The examiner explained there is evidence of an association between GERD and TERA exposure in the medical literature, and noted outside risk factors that would outweigh risks identified by TERA.  After noting the association between GERD and TERA, the examiner found the Veteran has no outside risk factors for the development of GERD.  

There is both positive and negative evidence as to whether the Veteran has a current diagnosis of GERD and there is positive and negative evidence as to whether the Veteran's GERD is related to service (including TERA).  The evidence is nearly balanced as to whether the Veteran has a diagnosis of GERD that is related to service.  Thus, all reasonable doubt is resolved in the Veteran's favor, and service connection for GERD is granted.  

2. Entitlement to service connection for gastroenteritis

In February 1974, the Veteran was noted to have gastroenteritis, with the etiology undetermined.  In April 1975, he had complaints of stomach pain for 3 to 4 days and was noted to have a history of peptic ulcer disease.  In September 1979, he complained of severe stomach pain and discomfort.  He had classic peptic ulcer disease symptoms of epigastric pain.  He reported chronic mid-epigastric pain since 1967.  In November 1979, he was noted to have a peptic ulcer with severe pyloric spasm.  He was noted to have a long history of dyspepsia dating back many years.    

In January 2018, he underwent an esophageal examination.  He was diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease during service and had been taking Tagamet for the condition which is also the same medication to treat GERD.  The examiner stated there are no objective findings of chronic GERD, and concluded it is less likely as not that the Veteran's current GI complaints were caused by or related to service. 

At the Board hearing he reported experiencing gastrointestinal discomfort during service that has continued to present.  He is in receipt of service connection for a duodenal ulcer.

In January 2023, the Veteran underwent an examination.  The examiner explained the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis.  The examiner noted that gastroenteritis is typically a short-term infectious illness of the gastrointestinal tract with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever.  It can be viral or bacterial and is typically short lived.  The examiner indicated that duodenal ulcer is not known to cause or contribute to the development of gastroenteritis.  During service, he had one episode of acute gastroenteritis.  The Veteran is currently prescribed famotidine.  Famotidine is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, erosive esophagitis, and GERD.  The examiner noted the records do not show for which pathology the Veteran's famotidine is prescribed.  The examiner found no evidence to support a diagnosis of chronic gastroenteritis while the Veteran served active duty, or post-separation.  History or symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis are not noted at the 1992 retirement physical.  Therefore, the examiner concluded that gastroenteritis was less likely than not caused by his duodenal ulcer.  Further, gastroenteritis was less likely than not related to exposure to herbicide agents such as Agent Orange.  

In a July 2023 addendum, the examiner concluded gastroenteritis is less likely than not related to service.  The examiner explained there is no current chronic condition of gastroenteritis found on exam, and the condition is not known to be caused by herbicide exposure.  The examiner found that the Veteran does not have gastroenteritis but noted that he is currently taking medications to treat other gastrointestinal symptoms.  The examiner did not; however, clarify the nature of these gastrointestinal symptoms and whether they could be the result of service in SW Asia.

In a November 2023 opinion, the examiner stated the Veteran does not have an intestinal condition.  The examiner concluded the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis.  Records show the Veteran had one occasion of gastroenteritis during service.  He is currently prescribed famotidine, which is indicated for the treatment of stomach ulcers, esophagitis, and GERD.  The records do not show for which pathology famotidine is prescribed.  Gastroenteritis was less likely than not related to an event, injury, or disease in active duty.  The examiner concluded the claimed condition was less likely than not caused by the indicated toxic exposure risk activities, after considering the total potential exposure through all applicable military deployments of the Veteran and the synergistic, combined effect of all toxic exposure risk activities of the Veteran.  There is no pathology to warrant a diagnosis that can be related to the claimed toxic exposure.  To conclude, the claimed condition of gastroenteritis is less likely than not related to an event injury or disease in service.  The examiner concluded there is no functional gastrointestinal disorder pathology or condition, and he does not have gastroenteritis.  

In May 2024, the Veteran underwent an examination and the examiner concluded there is no evidence of gastroenteritis, or a gastrointestinal disorder.  The examiner stated there is no pathology to warrant a diagnosis or condition that can be related to the claimed condition of gastroenteritis.  

In a separate May 2024 opinion, the examiner noted the Veteran's medical history and concluded the Veteran does not have a diagnosis of gastroenteritis.  He reported a history of heartburn, acidic taste in mouth, and nausea, and treats with Famotidine.  The examiner explained the Veteran has GERD, which is a disease with a clear and specific etiology and diagnosis. 

Given the overwhelming evidence of record, the evidence does not indicate the Veteran has a diagnosis of gastroenteritis during the appeal period.  The Veteran had an acute and transitory episode of gastroenteritis during service, that did not persist post-service.  The January 2023 examiner found the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis and noted the Veteran's acute and transitory episode of gastroenteritis during service.  Thus, the January 2023 examiner found, there is no direct link to service, or to exposure to herbicide agents.  

As for the claim of a nexus to his SW Asia service, although he served during the Persian Gulf War, he cannot establish service connection for an undiagnosed illness under 38 C.F.R. § 3.317, because there is no indication of a chronic disability as to a gastrointestinal disorder that manifests as gastroenteritis.  As was found by the November 2023 examiner, the Veteran does not have symptoms consistent with gastroenteritis, and concluded the claimed condition was less likely than not caused by a TERA activity.  There is no pathology to warrant a diagnosis that can be related to the claimed toxic exposure. 

The Board considered the Veteran's reports regarding his gastrointestinal symptoms, which he is competent to report.  However, the Board finds the persuasive evidence is against the Veteran's claim for service connection for gastroenteritis, or a functional gastrointestinal condition.  Although the Veteran believes he suffers from gastroenteritis symptoms that are related to an in-service injury, he is not competent to provide a nexus opinion in this case.  The record does not reflect that he has the requisite training or expertise to offer a medical opinion diagnosing a gastrointestinal condition and linking his current symptoms to an in-service injury and as such he is not competent to provide an opinion in this case.  Jandreau v. Nicholson, 492 F.3d 1372, 1377 (Fed. Cir. 2007).

The medical evidence is more probative and more credible than the lay opinions of record.  The January 2023 and November 2023 VA examination did not find any indication of a gastrointestinal disorder on examination with the exception of the diagnosis of GERD.  Further, the treatment records are absent for an indication of a gastroenteritis.  Thus, the more persuasive evidence of record indicates the Veteran does not have gastroenteritis or a functional gastrointestinal disorder, to include as due to service in Vietnam and/or SW Asia, and service connection is not warranted.

?

As such, the Board finds that service connection for gastroenteritis is not warranted.  As the persuasive evidence is against the claim, the benefit of the doubt rule is not applicable.  For these reasons, the claim is denied.

 

 

H.M. WALKER

Veterans Law Judge

Board of Veterans' Appeals

Attorney for the Board	Skiouris, Elena

The Board's decision in this case is binding only with respect to the instant matter decided. This decision is not precedential and does not establish VA policies or interpretations of general applicability. 38 C.F.R. § 20.1303.
